title: Mortgages
description: Fixed and adjustable loans, where the payment goes, and when a refinance pays off.
wolfLine: The rate is the headline. The cash to close and the break-even are the decision.

adjustable-rate-mortgage.definition: A mortgage whose interest rate can change after a starter period. The payment can rise.
adjustable-rate-mortgage.example: An ARM at $1,100 a month for five years. The estimate says it could become $1,450.

amortization.definition: The schedule that splits each mortgage payment into interest and principal. Early payments are mostly interest.
amortization.example: A $1,200 payment. The first month, $1,000 is interest and $200 is principal.

mortgage-points.definition: An upfront fee equal to 1% of the loan for each point. You pay it at closing to get a lower rate. It pays off only if you keep the loan long enough.
mortgage-points.example: One point on a $200,000 loan is $2,000.

refinancing.definition: Replacing your mortgage with a new one, usually to lower the rate or the payment. You pay closing costs again.
refinancing.example: A refinance that costs $4,000 and saves $100 a month takes 40 months to break even.

lessons.title: What You Are Paying
lessons.summary: A mortgage is the loan. The payment is not all principal.

steps.title: The loan, named
steps.body:
A [[mortgage]] is a loan to buy a home, usually paid over 15 or 30 years. The house is the collateral.

Each payment has [[interest]] and [[principal]]. On a **$200,000** loan, a **$1,200** payment can send most of the early dollars to interest.

steps.prompt: What is a mortgage?
choices: A loan used to buy a home, paid back over many years
The cash you pay up front so you borrow less
A fee the seller pays at closing
steps.explain: The down payment is the cash up front. The mortgage is what you still owe.

steps.prompt: What is the collateral on a home loan?
steps.explain: If you do not pay, the lender can take the house.

steps.prompt: The first payments on a typical mortgage are mostly principal.
steps.explain: They are mostly interest. Principal is the smaller slice at the start.

steps.prompt: The part of the payment that reduces what you owe is the ___.
steps.explain: Principal pays the loan down. Interest is the cost of borrowing.

lessons.title: Fixed or Adjustable
lessons.summary: The cheaper payment today can be the expensive one later.

steps.context: A fixed rate keeps the same [[interest]] rate. An [[adjustable-rate mortgage]] can change after the starter period.

steps.prompt: You will keep the loan for 30 years and you need a payment that cannot jump. Which page fits?
why: The rate and the payment stay.
Nothing freezes an ARM at the starter payment.
steps.explain: The fixed page stays at $1,200. The adjustable page says it can become $1,450.

steps.prompt: The adjustable payment on this page is promised for all 30 years.
steps.explain: It is promised for the starter period. After that it can rise.

steps.prompt: The loan whose rate can change is the ___ one.
steps.explain: Adjustable means it can move. Fixed means it stays.

lessons.title: 15 Years or 30
lessons.summary: The shorter loan costs more each month and less in interest.

steps.title: This lender’s estimate
steps.body:
Same **$200,000** loan. The 30-year estimate charges **$232,000** of interest over the life of the loan. The 15-year estimate charges **$104,000**.

The 30-year payment shown is **$1,200**. The 15-year payment shown is **$1,700**. These are the lender’s figures, not a formula to memorize.

steps.prompt: How much less interest does the 15-year estimate charge?
How much more is the 15-year payment each month?
What do you pay extra each year if you take the 15-year payment?
steps.explain: $500 × 12 = $6,000 a year, in exchange for far less interest over the life of the loan.

steps.prompt: The 30-year loan is cheaper in total interest on this estimate.
steps.explain: It is cheaper each month. Over the life of the loan it costs $128,000 more in interest.

lessons.title: Where the Payment Goes
lessons.summary: Early on, you are mostly paying for the loan, not paying it off.

steps.title: One month, up close
steps.body:
[[Amortization]] splits the payment. Balance **$200,000**. This month’s interest is **$1,000**. The payment is **$1,200**.

Later, interest is **$600** on a smaller balance, and more of the same $1,200 hits principal.

steps.prompt: Payment $1,200 and interest $1,000. How much principal do you pay this month?
The balance was $200,000. After that $200 of principal, what do you owe?
A later month: interest is $600 of the same $1,200 payment. How much is principal then?
Why does the early payment feel slow?
choices: The lender keeps the principal and applies it at the end
Principal is optional in the first five years
steps.explain: The interest is the cost of a large balance. As the balance falls, the interest slice shrinks.

lessons.title: Points
lessons.summary: You pay interest up front for a lower rate later.

steps.title: One point, one percent
steps.body:
One [[points|mortgage-points]] is **1%** of the loan, paid at closing. On **$200,000**, one point is **$2,000**.

In this example it saves **$50** a month. You need **40** months to get the $2,000 back. If you sell before that, the point was a loss.

steps.prompt: What is one point on a $200,000 loan?
The point saves $50 a month. How many months to earn back $2,000?
You sell after 24 months. How much of the $2,000 have the monthly savings not covered yet?
Points are always worth it because a lower rate is always better.
steps.explain: They are worth it if you keep the loan past the break-even month. A short stay can make them a loss.

lessons.title: The Loan Estimate
lessons.summary: The shopping page. Compare it before you fall in love with a house.

steps.title: Read the cash, not just the rate
steps.body:
A Loan Estimate shows the loan, the monthly principal and interest, the [[closing costs]], and the cash to close.

This one is a **$200,000** loan. Cash to close is the **$40,000** [[down payment]] plus **$6,000** of costs.

steps.prompt: What is the estimated cash to close?
What is the monthly principal and interest on this estimate?
steps.explain: The page lists it: $1,200. Tax and insurance are not in that line.

steps.prompt: Two lenders offer the same rate. One’s closing costs are $2,000 higher. What is the honest comparison?
choices: The higher closing costs make that loan more expensive up front
The rates match, so the loans match
steps.explain: The rate is one line. The cash to close is another.

steps.prompt: The $1,200 line is your whole housing payment, including tax and insurance.
steps.explain: It is principal and interest only. Escrow for tax and insurance would be extra.

lessons.title: Refinancing
lessons.summary: A new loan is worth it when the savings outlast the costs.

steps.title: Pay the cover charge again
steps.body:
[[Refinancing]] replaces the old [[mortgage]] with a new one. This example costs **$4,000** to close and saves **$100** a month.

Break-even is **40** months. A move in two years does not get there.

steps.prompt: Closing costs are $4,000 and you save $100 a month. How many months to break even?
You will move in 24 months. How short of the 40-month break-even is that?
steps.explain: 40 − 24 = 16 months short.

steps.prompt: You will move in two years. What does this example say?
choices: Do not refinance. You will not earn back the $4,000
Refinance, because any lower rate is a win
Refinance and roll the $4,000 in so it becomes free
steps.explain: Rolling the cost into the loan does not erase it. You still pay it, with interest.

steps.prompt: A refinance with a lower rate is free if you do not write a check at closing.
steps.explain: The cost can be added to the loan. It is still a cost.

lessons.title: Extra Payments
lessons.summary: A small extra payment hits principal. It is not a fee.

story.title: Luis pays a little extra
story.body:
Luis is 34. His required principal and interest is **$1,200**. He adds **$100** when the month allows.

In a month where interest is **$1,000**, the required principal is **$200**. The extra $100 makes that month’s principal **$300**.

He does not send the extra $100 if it would empty his emergency fund. A paid-down loan is a poor trade for a car repair you cannot cover.

steps.prompt: Luis adds $100 a month. How much extra principal is that in a year?
Interest is $1,000 of a $1,200 payment. With no extra, how much is principal?
He adds $100 that month. How much principal does he pay?
The emergency fund is down to one week of expenses. Should he send the extra $100?
choices: Yes. Principal always outranks a cushion
Yes, but put the $100 on a credit card
steps.explain: The extra payment is optional. The cushion is what keeps a surprise from becoming debt.

steps.prompt: An extra principal payment is the same thing as buying points.
steps.explain: Points are an upfront fee for a lower rate. An extra payment reduces the balance directly.
